5-2.title: Patterns When Multiplying a Whole Number by Powers of 10

questions.title: Problem 1 · Pennies in a 1-inch stack
questions.hint: Find the stack that is labeled 1 in.
steps: Look at the four stacks of pennies.
Find the stack whose height is marked 1 in.
Read how many pennies are in that stack.
questions.answer: 17 pennies
questions.verification: Read from the penny stacks on the page (17 pennies = 1 in.).

questions.title: Problem 1 · Pennies in a 2-inch stack
questions.hint: Find the stack that is labeled 2 in.
steps: Find the stack whose height is marked 2 in.
Read how many pennies it has.
Check: 2 inches is double 1 inch, and 17 × 2 = 34.
questions.answer: 34 pennies
questions.verification: Read from the penny stacks on the page (34 pennies = 2 in.); checked 17 × 2 = 34 in Python.

questions.title: Problem 2 · Pennies in a 1-foot stack
questions.hint: A foot is 12 inches.
questions.answer: About 204 pennies (17 × 12 = 204).
questions.verification: Computed in Python; 17 × 12 = 204; checked 34 × 6 = 204.

questions.title: Problem 3 · Guess: a mile-high stack
questions.hint: This is a guess, so just think about how big the number might be.
steps: A mile is 5,280 feet, and each foot has about 200 pennies.
Think: is the answer in the thousands, the millions, or the billions?
Write your best guess. It does not have to be exact.
questions.answer: Sample answer: about 1,000,000 pennies. Any sensible guess is fine; the calculated estimate is about 1,077,120.
questions.verification: Guess prompt; reference value 204 × 5,280 = 1,077,120 computed in Python.

questions.title: Problem 3 · A number that is too large
questions.hint: Pick a number much, much bigger than a mile of pennies could be.
steps: Remember a mile-high stack needs about a million pennies.
Choose a number that is far bigger, like billions.
questions.answer: Sample answer: 1,000,000,000 (one billion) is definitely too large.
questions.verification: Open-ended; 1,000,000,000 > 1,077,120 by far (checked in Python).

questions.title: Problem 3 · A number that is too small
questions.hint: Pick a number that could not even reach the top of a tall building.
steps: Choose a number that would make a stack far shorter than a mile, like a few thousand.
questions.answer: Sample answer: 1,000 pennies is definitely too small (that is only about 5 feet tall).
questions.verification: Open-ended; 1,000 ÷ 204 ≈ 4.9 feet, computed in Python.

questions.title: Problem 4 · Calculated estimate for a mile
questions.hint: Use your answer from Problem 2 and the number of feet in a mile.
questions.answer: About 1,077,120 pennies (204 × 5,280). About 1 million pennies.

questions.title: Be Curious · How are they the same?
questions.hint: Find the value of each expression and compare.
steps: 10,000 is the same as 10 × 10 × 10 × 10, which is 10⁴.
Notice what is the same and what is written differently.
questions.answer: Sample answer: They are the same because they all equal 150,000. They are different because they are written in different ways: with 10,000, with four factors of 10, with an exponent, and as a standard number.
questions.verification: Computed in Python; 15 × 10,000 = 15 × 10⁴ = 150,000.

questions.title: Math is… Mindset · Avoiding distractions
questions.hint: This is about you, so there is no wrong answer.
steps: Think about what pulls your attention away while you work.
Write one thing you do to stay focused.
questions.answer: Sample answer: I put away things I don't need and work in a quiet spot.
questions.verification: Personal reflection; no single correct answer.

questions.title: Math is… Structure · Why do digits shift?
questions.hint: Think about place value: each place is worth 10 times the place to its right.
steps: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth 10 times as much.
So each digit moves one place to the left.
A zero fills the empty ones place.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right, so multiplying by 10 makes every digit move one place to the left.
questions.verification: Place-value reasoning checked: 36 × 10 = 360 in Python.

questions.title: Work Together · 32 × 10², 10³, 10⁴
questions.hint: The exponent tells you how many zeros to put after 32.
steps: Each time the exponent goes up by 1, the product gets one more zero.
questions.answer: 32 × 10² = 3,200; 32 × 10³ = 32,000; 32 × 10⁴ = 320,000. The number of zeros after 32 equals the exponent.
questions.verification: Computed in Python; 32 × 100 = 3,200, 32 × 1,000 = 32,000, 32 × 10,000 = 320,000; checked by counting zeros.

questions.title: 13 · Relationship between the equations
questions.hint: Look at how the exponent changes and how the product changes.
steps: Each equation multiplies 6 by a power of 10.
The exponent goes 5, 7, 9: it grows by 2 each time.
Count the zeros in each product: 5, 7, 9.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Each exponent is 2 more than the one before, so each product has 2 more zeros and is 100 times as great. The number of zeros in each product equals the exponent.

questions.title: 14 · Carol's error
questions.hint: Count the zeros in 10,000 and in Carol's answer.
steps: 10,000 has 4 zeros, and 80 already has 1 zero.
So the product should have 1 + 4 = 5 zeros.
questions.answer: Carol is not correct. 80 × 10,000 = 800,000. She forgot to count the zero in 80.

questions.title: 16 · Extend Your Thinking · ? × 10⁵ = 56,300,000
questions.hint: 10⁵ adds 5 zeros to the end of the unknown factor.
steps: Take 5 zeros off the end of 56,300,000.
questions.answer: 563. Multiplying by 10⁵ puts 5 zeros after the factor, so remove 5 zeros from 56,300,000 to get 563.

questions.title: Reflect · Patterns with powers of 10
questions.hint: Think about the number of zeros and the exponent.
steps: Look back at the problems in this lesson.
What happened to the product each time you multiplied by 10?
How did the exponent tell you how many zeros to write?
questions.answer: Sample answer: The number of zeros added to the product is the same as the exponent, and each time you multiply by 10 the digits move one place to the left.
questions.verification: Reflection; pattern checked against Python products in this lesson.
